summary: Screw-pile light in the Potomac at Ragged Point: first lit 1910; wooden house dismantled 1962 for a skeletal tower on the same piles.

structures.type: hexagonal wood house on screw-pile foundation
skeletal tower on the original screw-pile foundation

access.note: Stands in the river on its own piles; no source describes a visit.

events.note: Act of 20 June 1906 authorised the light and fog signal.
Hexagonal wood house on seven wrought-iron piles; contractor finished 26 February 1910.
First shown 15 March 1910, a fourth-order lens flashing white every ten seconds.
Ice floes in the winter of 1917-18 damaged screw-pile lights in the Chesapeake and the Potomac; 600 tons of riprap placed at Ragged Point 1918-19.
Keeper Charles A. Larsen and assistant James A. Downs assisted the barge L. B. Adams, 28 November 1918.
Keeper Carl Geiling awarded the Lighthouse Service efficiency flag (Chapter dates 1923; Bulletin index lists the entry).
Radio sets from a New York donor distributed in the Baltimore district; Ragged Point received one.
Wooden house dismantled July 1962; skeletal tower with an automated light erected on the original screw-pile foundation.

corrections.why: The Board's account, excerpted by Chance Heritage Trust, and the Chapter timeline both give first lighting on 15 March 1910. The 1962 date marks the dismantling of the wooden house and the erection of the skeletal tower. The Wikidata 1962 first_lit is an error.

corrections.proposed: wooden house built 1910, dismantled July 1962; skeletal tower on the original screw-pile foundation
corrections.why: The wooden house is no longer standing; the structure on the foundation is a skeletal tower erected in 1962.

corrections.proposed: to verify against the Coast Guard Light List (2-16940)
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends describes a modern light shown from the tower on the foundation. The record's inactive status needs checking against the current List.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's first year of 1962 (Wikidata) and 1910 (USLHS) are both explained: 1910 is the first lighting; 1962 is the year the wooden house was dismantled and the skeletal tower erected.

OpenStreetMap maps a structure at the site, and LighthouseFriends reports the 1910 house dismantled in 1962. The structure now standing is the 1962 skeletal tower on the original foundation, so both sources are describing different things.

The Board's reports of 1896 and 1901 call the station Virginia; the Board's reports from 1907 call it Maryland (the 1907 heading as LighthouseFriends prints it; the 1909 heading in Chance Heritage Trust's excerpts); the Commissioner's 1918 list gives Maryland; the Chapter's heritage page places it at Coles Point on the Virginia shore. The sources do not settle the question, and the story uses Maryland, as the later reports do.

notes_for_editor: (1) Name conflict: the USLHS roster (cite 1) lists James S. Downs as first assistant from 1918 and as head keeper 1927-1930; the Commissioner-era Bulletin of 1919 (cite 7) reads the assistant at Ragged Point as James A. Downs. Matched by name only; the story says neither source settles the initial. (2) The Bulletin of 1919 OCR (scan of the Commissioner's bound report, cite 5, scan p. 460) places 'William McDorman, assistant keeper' beside the Ragged Point entry in a column I could not confidently assign; not used. (3) The 1906 to 1910 construction details and the 1910 lighting come from Chance Heritage Trust's excerpts (cite 12) and LighthouseFriends (cite 13), which quote the Board's FY1907, FY1909 and FY1910 reports. Those reports are not in the local corpus, so those lines were checked only against the secondary text; a primary check is still needed. (4) The Coast Guard Historian's Ragged Point (MD) page (history.uscg.mil article 1983218) and the Virginia-filed page (article 2015083) could not be read: the archived copy returned only a title. A search snippet from the MD page mentions a 1960s aircraft strafing and the keepers' response; it is unverified and not used. Wikipedia repeats the strafing without a source, so it is not used. (5) Focal height and characteristic in the record (4.6 m, Fl W 4s) differ from Wikipedia (13.5 m, Fl W 6s) with no source I could read for either; check the Coast Guard Light List. (6) Chance Heritage Trust's data sheet gives 'Commissioned Oct 1, 1908'; the Board's account gives first lighting in March 1910; the story follows the Board's account. (7) The Board reports call the station Virginia to at least 1901; the Commissioner's reports say Maryland by 1918. The record's state field should be checked against a current chart before publishing. (8) Photos: none added. The record's Wikimedia Commons image is unlicensed in the record and was not checked. (9) Verification 2026-10-28, matched by position in OCR'd text, not read on the page image: the $30,000 row of the 1901 appropriations table (cite 3, scan p. 65) and the 'James A. Downs' name in the 1919 Bulletin (cite 7, prose, not a table). The $30,000 figure also appears in the Board's 1901 narrative as LighthouseFriends prints it, and Downs's initial A. appears in the Commissioner's 1919 list and the Bulletin's 1918-1923 index.
